'''Anne Penfold Street''' {{post-nominals|country=AUS|AM}} (11 October 1932 – 28 December 2016) was one of Australia's leading mathematicians,{{r|wisenet}} specialising in [[combinatorics]]. She was the third woman to become a mathematics professor in Australia, following [[Hanna Neumann]] and [[Cheryl Praeger]].{{r|apsa|bcc}} She was the author of several textbooks,{{r|vale}} and her work on [[sum-free set]]s became a standard reference for its subject matter.{{r|payne}} She helped found several important organizations in combinatorics, developed a researcher network, and supported young students with interest in mathematics.{{r|vale}}

==Early life and education==
Anne Penfold Street was born on 11 October 1932 in [[Melbourne]],{{r|eas}} the daughter of a medical researcher.{{r|wisenet}} She earned a bachelor's degree in chemistry from the [[University of Melbourne]] in 1954,{{r|eas|praeger}} while working there as a tutor in chemistry{{r|eas}} and also studying mathematics.{{r|praeger}} She finished a master's degree in chemistry at Melbourne in 1956.{{r|vale|eas|donovan}} During this time she married another Melbourne chemist, Norman Street, and in 1957 the Streets and their young daughter moved to the [[University of Illinois at Urbana–Champaign]] where Norman Street had a new job.{{r|praeger}}

At Illinois, Street took up mathematics again.{{r|praeger}} After moving to [[Mildura]] and then returning to Urbana, she completed her doctorate at the University of Illinois in 1966, with a dissertation on [[group theory]] supervised by [[Michio Suzuki (mathematician)|Michio Suzuki]].{{r|donovan|mgp|ica}}

==Career==
After earning her doctorate, Street became a lecturer at the [[University of Queensland]] in 1967. While continuing to hold this position, she took a year of postdoctoral research at the [[University of Alberta]], and on her return to Queensland in 1970 was promoted to senior lecturer, promoted again to reader in 1975, and given a personal chair as professor in 1985.{{r|eas|praeger|donovan}}
At Queensland, she directed the Centre for Discrete Mathematics and Computing from its formation in 1998 until 2004.{{r|donovan}}

She also held visiting positions at the [[University of Waterloo]], [[University of Reading]], [[University of Manitoba]], [[University of Illinois at Urbana–Champaign]], [[University of Western Australia]], [[Auburn University]], and [[University of Canterbury]].{{r|eas}}

==Service to mathematics==
Street became the founding editor-in-chief of the ''Australasian Journal of Combinatorics'' in 1990, and continued to serve as editor-in-chief until 2001.{{r|vale|donovan}}

She helped found the [[Institute of Combinatorics and its Applications]] (ICA), became one of its founding fellows, and served as an editor of the ''Bulletin of the ICA'' from its founding in 1991 until 2014.{{r|praeger|donovan|ica}} She was president of the ICA from 1996 to 2002.{{r|vale|praeger|donovan}}

She was the founding president of the [[Combinatorial Mathematics Society of Australasia]], for the 1997–1998 term.{{r|vale|praeger}}

She also served as president of the Australian Mathematical Olympiad Committee from 1996 to 2001.{{r|praeger|donovan}}

==Awards and honours==
The [[Australian Mathematics Trust]] gave Street a [[B. H. Neumann Award for Excellence in Mathematics Enrichment]] in 1994.{{r|apsa|donovan|ica}}

The [[University of Waterloo]] gave her an [[honorary doctorate]] in 1996.{{r|apsa|praeger|donovan}}

In 1999, the Combinatorial Mathematics Society of Australasia gave her their inaugural medal for outstanding service.{{r|praeger|ica}}

She was named a [[Member of the Order of Australia]] in the [[2014 Queen's Birthday Honours (Australia)|2014 Queen's Birthday Honours]],{{r|vale|praeger}} primarily for her work with the [[Australian Mathematics Trust]] and the Australian Mathematical Olympiad Committee.{{r|donovan}}

==Personal life==
Street's daughter, [[Deborah J. Street]], is a statistician at the [[University of Technology Sydney]],{{r|wisenet}} and the coauthor (with her mother) of a book on the combinatorial [[design of experiments]].{{r|praeger|cxd}} Her son, Tony Street, is a researcher in Islamic Studies at the [[University of Cambridge]].{{r|praeger}}

==Death and legacy==
Street died on 28 December 2016.{{r|vale|praeger}}

The Anne Penfold Street Awards of the [[Australian Mathematical Society]], an initiative to provide family care for travelling mathematicians, are named after her.{{r|apsa|bcc|praeger}}

Beginning in 2016, the best student paper award from the annual Australasian Conference on Combinatorial Mathematics and Combinatorial Computing (ACCMCC) became known as the CMSA Anne Penfold Street Student Prize.{{r|donovan}}

==Books==
*''Combinatorics: Room Squares, Sum-Free Sets, Hadamard Matrices'' (with W. D. Wallis and [[Jennifer Seberry|Jennifer Seberry Wallis]], Springer, Lecture Notes in Mathematics 292, 1972){{r|payne}}
*''Combinatorial Theory: An Introduction'' (with W. D. Wallis, Charles Babbage Research Centre, 1977){{r|sheehan}}
*''Combinatorics: A First Course'' (with W. D. Wallis, Charles Babbage Research Centre, 1982){{r|c1c}}
*''[[Combinatorics of Experimental Design]]'' (with Deborah J. Street, Oxford University Press, 1987){{r|cxd}}
*''Discrete Mathematics: Logic and Structures'' (with Elizabeth J. Billington, Melbourne: Longman Cheshire, 1990; 2nd ed., 1993){{r|dmls}}
